title: Accelerating New Power Plants Depends on Better Data
gist: U.S. electricity demand is rising again as homes, vehicles, and data centers electrify, but there is no clear public picture of what it costs to build power plants by technology or location. RAND researchers argue this project-level cost data blackout leaves policymakers and investors unable to identify what raises prices or delays construction, and call for standardized federal cost-reporting published by the EIA.

insights.claim: U.S. electricity demand, stagnant for years, is now climbing as homes and vehicles electrify and data centers multiply, shifting the question from whether more power is needed to whether it can be built fast enough at an affordable price.
insights.speaker: Kelly Klima
insights.so_what: A structural demand inflection after years of flat load underpins bullish theses on generation, transmission, and grid-equipment names; the bottleneck migrates from demand to build-speed and cost.
insights.quote: Demand, stagnant for years, is climbing as homes and vehicles electrify and data centers multiply.
insights.locator: America is embarking on a vast build-out

insights.claim: The U.S. electric build-out is framed as a multitrillion-dollar effort, yet it is being debated with too little evidence on actual project costs.
insights.speaker: Kelly Klima
insights.so_what: Scale of capex signals a durable multi-year investment cycle for suppliers, but the evidence gap means headline cost estimates carry wide error bars investors should discount.
insights.quote: the public is left to debate a multitrillion-dollar build-out with too little evidence
insights.locator: Some limits on disclosure are reasonable

insights.claim: There is no clear public picture of what it costs to build power plants or how those costs vary across technologies and locations, an information gap that is slowing the U.S. energy build-out.
insights.speaker: Kelly Klima
insights.so_what: The core investable edge: whoever can source true project-level cost data has an informational advantage in siting, underwriting, and capital allocation that the market broadly lacks.
insights.quote: We do not have a clear public picture of what it costs to build power plants and how those costs vary among different technologies or locations.

insights.claim: Utility capital-expenditure disclosures, such as those from PG&E and Duke, are aggregated across the whole company and do not reliably show how much went to a gas plant, a solar farm, or a transmission upgrade.
insights.speaker: Kelly Klima
insights.so_what: Company-level capex in utility filings cannot be decomposed into per-project economics, so analysts modeling technology-specific returns are working from aggregates, not actuals.
insights.quote: the figures are usually aggregated across an entire company
insights.locator: The reason is that the relevant data

insights.claim: EIA and national-laboratory datasets, including Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's Generator Interconnection Costs and the Annual Technology Baseline, publish costs aggregated by state or region with plant-by-plant figures that are averages rather than actual project costs.
insights.speaker: Kelly Klima
insights.so_what: Even the most-cited public benchmarks are modeled averages, not observed spend, so cost curves built on them systematically miss project-level dispersion and outliers.
insights.quote: with plant-by-plant values representing average values rather than actual project costs

insights.claim: Private data platforms from Bloomberg, S&P Global, and ICF fill only part of the gap and often estimate project costs by applying broad assumptions to a project's generating capacity, useful as a rough benchmark but unable to explain cost differences.
insights.speaker: Kelly Klima
insights.so_what: Buyers of paid energy-cost data should probe methodology: much of what is sold as project-level cost is capacity-scaled estimation, not observed project spend.
insights.quote: even these services often estimate project costs by applying broad assumptions to a project's generating capacity

insights.claim: In one commercial platform RAND examined, over 90 percent of the facility costs recorded nationwide were simply a per-megawatt-installed number multiplied by nameplate capacity, which the authors call useless for understanding past or future project-cost trends.
insights.speaker: Kelly Klima
insights.so_what: A striking due-diligence flag: a headline share of advertised project-level cost data is synthetic capacity math, undercutting any analysis built on it.
insights.quote: over 90 percent of the costs recorded for facilities nationwide were in fact just a simple per-megawatt-installed number multiplied by the nameplate capacity of the facility
insights.locator: At RAND, we know this firsthand

insights.claim: In California and Massachusetts, higher labor costs, interconnection delays, and transmission upgrades can make power projects far more expensive than elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Kelly Klima
insights.so_what: State-level cost drivers materially change project IRR; developers and investors should weight interconnection and labor regimes heavily when siting capacity.
insights.quote: higher labor costs, interconnection delays, and transmission upgrades can make projects far more expensive

insights.claim: Texas combines lower costs with a comparatively streamlined permitting environment and has rapidly added wind and solar capacity, contrasting with high-cost coastal states.
insights.speaker: Kelly Klima
insights.so_what: Permitting speed and cost make Texas a structurally advantaged market for new renewables buildout, a location signal for capacity-siting and merchant-power exposure.
insights.quote: Texas, by contrast, combines lower costs with a comparatively streamlined permitting environment and has rapidly added wind and solar capacity

insights.claim: Federal policy can speed fossil-fuel production, support nuclear, and streamline major projects, but states and localities still determine where projects are sited, how long permitting takes, and what they cost.
insights.speaker: Kelly Klima
insights.so_what: Federal 'unleash energy' policy is necessary but not sufficient; the binding constraint on any given project remains local siting and permitting, so watch state-level rules more than federal headlines.
insights.quote: But states and localities still shape where projects are sited, how long they take to permit, and what they cost.

insights.claim: Without public project-level cost data, policymakers cannot confidently identify the barriers raising prices or delaying construction, and investors cannot easily distinguish manageable risks from expensive surprises.
insights.speaker: Kelly Klima
insights.so_what: The data gap directly translates into mispriced project risk; it is the mechanism by which cost overruns and delays surprise capital.
insights.quote: Investors cannot easily distinguish manageable risks from expensive surprises.

insights.claim: The authors recommend that Congress and federal agencies require standardized, project-level capital-cost reporting for energy projects receiving public funding or under federal jurisdiction, with the EIA publishing the results in a central repository.
insights.speaker: Kelly Klima
insights.so_what: If enacted, mandatory project-level cost transparency would reprice risk across the sector and erode the informational moat of incumbent private data vendors; a policy catalyst to watch.
insights.quote: Congress and federal agencies should require standardized, project-level capital-cost reporting for energy projects that receive public funding or operate under federal jurisdiction.

insights.claim: The authors frame better cost data not as new red tape but as making information the government already collects, plus information public investment makes possible, usable to decisionmakers.
insights.speaker: Kelly Klima
insights.so_what: Framing transparency as no-new-burden is the political path to adoption; a low-cost, high-impact reform that could clear regulatory bottlenecks.
insights.quote: it is a call to make the information government already collects—and the information public investment makes possible—useful to the people making consequential decisions
insights.locator: This is not a call for another layer
